generator.program.note: The lineage's own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the broadleaf base: it gives the values its species leave unset, which the broadleaf program gave as defaults until then.
The climbing program for the family's twining honeysuckles (Lonicera ciliosa, added 2026-10-18): the family's own program is on the broadleaf base, which has no host to climb.

traits.perianth.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334, 336: Ronse De Craene (Caprifoliaceae incl. Dipsacaceae, Valerianaceae): calyx and 5-lobed corolla, the calyx often a rim, teeth, bristles or absent (general formula K0-5 or many, C5).

traits.flower_merosity.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334, 336: corolla 5-lobed; most Dipsaceae 4-lobed by fusion of the two posterior petals. Simpson pp. 435, 438 agrees (5, rarely 4).

traits.stamens.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334, 336: stamens 1 to 5, rarely 5, mostly 4 (Dipsacus), 3 in Valeriana, down to 1 (Centranthus); Simpson p. 435 gives 5 for Lonicera and kin.

traits.carpels.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334: Ronse De Craene general formula: inferior ovary of 2 to 3, rarely 5 to 8, carpels; Simpson p. 435 gives 2 to 5 (to 8) for Caprifoliaceae s.s.

traits.ovary_position.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334: inferior ovary throughout the family; Simpson pp. 435, 438, 439 agree for all three segregates.

traits.corolla_shape.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 334: Ronse De Craene lists a tubular corolla among the family's defining features.

traits.hypanthium.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 435, 505: flowers epigynous, rarely epihypogynous. Simpson p. 505 defines hypogynous and epigynous as flowers without a hypanthium.

traits.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), families 48 Caprifoliaceae, 312 Valerianaceae and 313 Dipsacaceae, which APG joins as Caprifoliaceae (Sambucus and Viburnum go to Viburnaceae): leaves opposite, simple or deeply divided; flowers mostly in cymes, in heads in the teasels. The order's file states the opposite leaves, the missing stipules and the inferior ovary.

traits.leaf_habit.note: Wikipedia Caprifoliaceae (read 2026-10-17; ~860 spp, 33 genera): leaves evergreen or deciduous, no ranking. Its genus list gives Valeriana 426, Lonicera 158, Cephalaria 102, Scabiosa 68, Lomelosia 63, Knautia 55. The herbaceous majority (Valerianoideae and Dipsacoideae, ~700 spp) loses its leafy shoots each season, and Lonicera is mostly deciduous with an evergreen minority (Weigela, Symphoricarpos, Kolkwitzia deciduous too); evergreen leaves remain common in shrubby honeysuckles and some Abelia. Re-ranks the earlier value, from watson-dallwitz-1992, whose top states were tied.

traits.flower_symmetry.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data), family Caprifoliaceae with Carlemanniaceae, Dipsacaceae, Morinaceae, Sambucaceae, Valerianaceae: flowers regular or irregular as coded, a state the authors qualify keeping its word (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py).

traits.zygomorphy.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data), family Caprifoliaceae with Carlemanniaceae, Dipsacaceae, Morinaceae, Sambucaceae, Valerianaceae: its irregular flowers are of no named kind (pea flower, two lips, orchid lip), read from the coded corolla symmetry (spec-rework/b1/delta): zygomorphy other.

traits.leaf_arrangement.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 435, 437, family Caprifoliaceae: leaf arrangement opposite; read as "opposite".

traits.stipules.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 435, 437, family Caprifoliaceae: stipules false (or reduced), usually; read as {"false": "usually"}.

traits.fruit_type.note: APweb, Dipsacales page, Caprifoliaceae (read 2026-10-16): of about 890 species, Dipsacoideae (about 290) have a dry one-seeded fruit and Linnaeoideae (20) an achene, while only Caprifolieae (about 181) have berries (Lonicera) or drupes (Symphoricarpos); DELTA Valerianaceae adds an achene-like fruit for the roughly 400 valerians, so achene is the usual state.
